replies.author: random_boss
replies.body:
Here’s what I do, let’s compare notes:
* Durable files that track overall project status and current working state
* Orchestrator that takes what needs to be done now and hands it to subagents to plan, review, implement, or fix
* Strict usage cap of 250k tokens; the orchestrator replaces subagents who hit their cap, and when the orchestrator hits its cap, it writes everything out to the durable project files and retires, sending a notice to another agent (called a relay) whose only job is to watch for retiring orchestrators, then clears itself
* Relay agent gets the notice, then sends the next prompt to now-cleared former orchestrator and work continues
* Anything orchestrators need me to review, approve, test, or rule on goes to a special inbox I created that agents always check 

With this I basically set it and forget it and check my inbox intermittently for new builds to test or decisions it needs from me. The rest of the time it’s cranking away. Some workflows require much heavier iteration loops with me though, and I generally need to check things at least hourly, with a fairly large review in the morning for what it did overnight.

replies.author: StoneCypher
replies.body:
i'll call my current game `4x`, because it is a 4x.  my techniques for 4x have been different than for my earlier projects.

for 4x, i started by looking up around 120 similar games, and dispatching research sets to write down their features, their characters, their powerups, their game modes, their map resources, everything i could think of.  built a list of about 1200 things, where "luxury resource" is a thing, not the specific instances like silk.

then i went to opus, fable, gippity, gemini, and google search ai, fed them the list, and asked them what they thought was missing, what they thought were bad ideas, what they thought could be rephrased, reframed.  drove the list up to about 1400.

dropped the list to a json array of objects.  the list items became .origin; then they got a proper short title, a long description, a 1-5 ranking of importance, a category and subcategory, and a status (accepted declined complete underway partial needswork undefined.)

then i had each one filed as a ticket.  then on each ticket, i spent an opus 5.5 medium researching each ticket independently for each game.  that's about 500,000 research missions, which spent almost two weeks of account tokens.  the resulting issues were enormous and fascinating.

boiled that back down to a list of 1800 features.  had gippity rank the categories by what it thought a player would care about the most, then the subcategories, then the items within each subcategory.  had it make a little html interface so i could presbutan "accept" "decline" "accept" "fucking what?" "accept" for about two hours.  many bongs were ripped.  closed all the old issues in the process.

exported that as a new json.  opened a set of new issues, this time prioritized and ordered and much-better-detailed.  i have a repo which is just 300-ish issue labels; applied it to all the new issues.

went into gippity and told it to have an astra run a fleet of 15 sol mediums to do implementations.  it has claude vet each one on the way out.  had to try a couple times to figure out how to phrase it that they wouldn't just stop after the first set, but once you get to "please run 15 sol mediums against the issue list, driving each isue to a landed pr, then immediately spin up a new agent to replace the finished one" as a `/goal`, [they just start straight churning the list non-stop](https://imgur.com/a/cSuVsE4).

it's kind of breathtaking.  at the conceptual scale that "a feature" is railroads, or harbors, i've watched this fucker crank 700 features in the last 36 hours

the 4x i'm currently making has about 50% higher feature density than civ7.  it's ... it's wild.

In one project, I've been using Superpowers + a custom software engineering skill (with 4.x models until the recent release). In another, I'm using stock Opus 5.5.

The stock project feels like it's going quite a bit faster without any quality drop in the output that's obvious from playtesting. comments.author: taddeimania
comments.body:
I've been spending most of the week with Claude (Opus 5.5) building a new Everquest client in rust to use with custom EQEmulator servers. What started out as a "can a 1:1 replacement be built" turned into a "the sky is the limit on what is possible now".

Highlight of the week: I've always felt like Bards in Everquest should be able to play music that others can hear, so I had the agent update the server to support sending packets of midi between the clients and added a 3d model of a piano to a bard hall. Then added a 1 octave keyboard playable on a QWERTY keyboard and anyone walking by the guild hall could hear a bard hammering away on the piano. It \*blew my mind\* that it was capable of doing that.

So yeah, now i'm having it learn the questing/adventure system and planning on having it build custom campaigns for my brother and I to run through together.

While not directly AI game dev related, I DOOOO partake in creation and activities related to it.  Por ejemplo, I ended up creating a companion album to the game.

Y'see, I'm using Makeplay.ai to make the game, right?  Sure it's locked to the platform, but I own the IP, so I've got that going on for me.  During the month, however, they ended up closing up every loophole to upload and install your own music to the game, forcing us to rely on the AI for music and sound.

Now this is perfectly fine, it's just not the specific songs I've generated and edited.

To make a long story short I now have a companion album people can listen to earmarked for later use if the platform ever opens it up again or I have the thing developed off-site someday.

I also worked up an album of instrumental music to use for a future beatemup project, my next game, so there's that.

For context I mostly only use claude pro (chat) and lovable for protoyping general app, but am not sure on game or browser game. (i have no coding knowledge at all)

replies.author: caesium23
replies.body:
First: the more programming experience you have, the further you'll get. It may not be strictly necessary with the latest models, but it will help tremendously to understand how things are built, and why, so you have the option to tell the agent exactly *how* to build something, not just what, and keep it on track with stuff that will be easy to change and maintain later. 

That said, the easiest way to get started is to pick your favorite AI and *describe* the game you want it to build and ask it to make a plan: "Write a detailed plan to build a platformer that's like a cross between Mario and Sonic and Celeste only you can control gravity."

Then you can review what it comes up with and hash out the details before it actually builds anything. The more specific and detailed you can make the plan, the better.

Don't get too attached to that plan though. I guarantee some of the stuff you thought would be awesome will turn out to suck once you playtest it. Game dev is an iterative process.
